# 4.1 Introduction

## What You'll Learn in this Chapter

Welcome to Chapter 4! The reasoning skills you'll learn in this chapter
will broaden the range of arguments you'll be able to handle.

You'll learn more about **recognizing arguments**. In particular, you'll
learn:

-   how to recognize arguments that don't contain inference indicator
    expressions.

You'll learn more about **analyzing arguments**. In particular, you'll
learn:

-   how to recognize when multiple sentences in an argument convey the
    same claim, and
-   how to map arguments with independent reasons.

You'll learn more about **evaluating arguments**. In particular, you'll
learn:

-   how to evaluate inferences using inference forms, and
-   how to evaluate arguments with independent reasons.

You'll learn more about **constructing arguments**. In particular,
you'll learn:

-   how to construct arguments with independent reasons, and
-   how to write passages containing arguments with independent reasons.

## Independent Reasons

In Chapter 1, we learned about arguments that can be represented with
very short maps because the premise takes us directly to the ultimate
conclusion. Maps of these arguments are like maps that show how a
starting boulder and an ending boulder can be connected with a single
bridge.

![](/images/ch04/boulders_one_ladder.png){.illustration width=140px fig-alt="A bridge leads from a gray boulder up to a golden boulder."}

In Chapter 2, we learned about arguments with subconclusions. Maps of
these arguments are like maps that show how intermediate boulders can
help us work our way from the starting boulder to the ending boulder.

![](/images/ch04/boulders_subconclusion.png){.illustration width=125px fig-alt="A bridge leads from a gray boulder up to a second gray boulder, and another bridge leads from there up to a golden boulder."}

And in Chapter 3, the previous chapter, we saw arguments with dependent
reasons. Maps of these arguments are like maps that depict cases where
multiple boulders need to work together to support a bridge.

![](/images/ch04/boulders_dependent.png){.illustration width=200px fig-alt="Two gray boulders side by side, joined by a plank that rests on both of them. A single bridge rises from the plank up to a golden boulder."}

Have you noticed something? In all of these cases, there is only *one*
route to the golden boulder. And of course, real life isn't like that.
**In real life there are often multiple routes to a destination**, like
so:

![](/images/ch04/boulders_independent.png){.illustration width=190px fig-alt="Two separate gray boulders, each with its own bridge leading up to a golden boulder."}

Similarly, in real life, arguments often present us with different ways
to reach the ultimate conclusion. We'll call these different ways
"independent reasons" or "independent lines of reasoning." That's what
we'll be learning about next!

## Summary of Introduction

The big idea in this chapter will be independent reasons, each of which
supports a conclusion. This will give us independent lines of reasoning.
